video_title: CME's Terry Duffy on the Disconcerting State of Finance Regulation | Odd Lots
gist: Live in Chicago, CME Group CEO Terry Duffy (moving to executive chairman) argues the CFTC is rubber-stamping everything (2,500 self-certifications, zero denials) in non-durable agency actions; he attacks manipulable prediction contracts and perpetual futures as disguised swaps sought only for leverage, critiques Hyperliquid's no-KYC model, and pushes GPU futures and an inevitable but bank-constrained 24/7 market.

insights.claim: Terry Duffy says that since the second Trump administration began, about 2,500 self-certifications have been submitted to the CFTC and not a single one has been denied.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Signals near-zero CFTC gatekeeping on new contracts, lowering barriers for prediction-market and crypto entrants competing with CME.
insights.quote: there's been 2,500 self-certification that been submitted into the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Not one of them has been denied.

insights.claim: Duffy argues the CFTC and SEC are circumventing acts of Congress with agency rules that the next administration can erase with a pen stroke, so current deregulation is not durable.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Business models built on current agency-level permissions (prediction markets, perps, crypto) carry policy-reversal risk after the next election.
insights.quote: those are rules and regs of the agency that can be easily swiped away by away from a pen when the next administration comes in.

insights.claim: Duffy characterizes the current regulatory posture as a 'ready, fire' strategy where anything goes, which he finds disconcerting, while insisting smart balanced regulation is what grows confident markets.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Incumbent exchange CEO flags a lax regime that could end in a blow-up and backlash re-regulation.
insights.quote: it does feel a bit of a ready, fire strategy going on right now where anything can go. And so it's very disconcerting.

insights.claim: Duffy criticizes the President charging for faster access to information via Truth Social, arguing the President should release information to everyone at the same time.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Highlights information-asymmetry risks from paid early-access feeds tied to political figures.
insights.quote: You're supposed to give information to all of us at the same time, not not have a feed to get your information quicker so others can act on it.

insights.claim: Duffy argues contracts like how many hot dogs Joey Chestnut eats at Nathan's, or whether George Santos attends the State of the Union, violate CFTC Core Principle 3 because they are readily susceptible to manipulation and have no economic purpose.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Novelty event contracts are the most legally exposed piece of prediction-market platforms if enforcement tightens.
insights.quote: how is it not in violation of Core Principle Three, which is susceptible, readily susceptible to manipulation?

insights.claim: Duffy rejects the prediction-market argument that insider trading adds informational value, saying a level playing field on information is what the industry has fought for and markets lose credibility otherwise.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Insider-trading tolerance is a reputational and regulatory fault line for prediction-market venues.
insights.quote: So to say that insider information could be a good thing and anything is affordable to me.

insights.claim: Duffy classifies sports event contracts (e.g., LeBron James rebounds) as gambling with no economic impact, and says legitimate contracts need a natural buyer and seller such as a commercial and a producer.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Frames a hedger-based test that sports event contracts fail, implying they belong under state gambling regulation.
insights.quote: most contracts need to have a natural buyer, a natural shower commercial and a producer of that product in order to facilitate a contract.

insights.claim: CME partnered with Australian firm Future Sports on a sports index product where every team starts at 7500 and moves with performance, similar to the S&P 500, which Duffy says lets team owners monetize value without selling.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: CME's answer to sports betting is an index-based hedging product with a commercial use case, a potential new revenue line.
insights.quote: Every team starts out at 7500 and you go up and down, never depending on performance.

insights.claim: Duffy says CME has done deals with the NBA and MLB around the Future Sports index products.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: League partnerships give CME a legitimate sports-exposure product with institutional backing.
insights.quote: now we just did a deal with the NBA. We've done a deal with MLB

themes.theme: Perpetual futures are swaps in disguise

insights.claim: Duffy argues perpetual futures are legally swaps because their funding rate involves two parties paying each other, so the CFTC's approval of Bitcoin perps as futures circumvented Congress and is the basis of CME's litigation with the CFTC.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: CME litigation could reclassify US-listed perps as swaps, undermining competitors' perp products.
insights.quote: in the definition of a swap anytime two parties page other it's deemed as well. So they circumvented Congress.

insights.claim: Duffy contrasts futures' Section 1256 tax treatment (60% long-term / 40% short-term gains) with swaps taxed as ordinary income, plus swap-specific margin, clearing and dealer registration requirements, making the classification economically decisive.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Perp classification determines tax and compliance burden, a regulatory arbitrage edge for whoever gets futures treatment.
insights.quote: get what's called 1256 tax treatment, which is 60 long term 40 short terms and gains.

insights.claim: CME did not list a 24/7 perpetual oil contract; instead it pursued a small 10-barrel 24/7 oil futures contract to compete with offshore platforms that US participants can access via VPN with no one policing it.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: CME is moving into small-size, round-the-clock products to fight offshore retail leakage.
insights.quote: I just put for 24/7 oil on a ten barrel contract, very small contract, just to compete with some of the platforms that are being traded overseas

insights.claim: Duffy says institutions cannot manage risk with perps because there is no expiration date and the funding-rate timing (once a day, twice, hourly) is set arbitrarily, while corporations need a date certain against loans and hedges.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Perps are unlikely to win institutional hedging flow, limiting them to retail speculation.
insights.quote: So institutions go, this is impossible for us to trade.

insights.claim: Duffy contends perps are being brought to the US for leverage and leverage only, and the next push will be leveraged sports prediction contracts and single-stock perpetuals, which he calls potentially catastrophic for risk management.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Expect product pushes toward leveraged single-stock and sports perps, and associated tail risk.
insights.quote: They're they're trying to be brought here for leverage and leverage only.

insights.claim: Duffy says roughly 98% of Hyperliquid's business is done via Trade XYZ deployer markets, with Hyperliquid itself listing only crypto, and rejects founder Jeff Yan's argument that only users/deployers need regulation.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Most Hyperliquid volume sits in deployer-listed non-crypto products, the part most exposed to US legal challenge.
insights.quote: which is what 98% of hyper liquid business is done by trade x, y, z

insights.claim: Duffy argues Hyperliquid's lack of KYC, auto-liquidation, and leverage up to 250% on some products can cause cascading liquidations and market-moving events, violating CFTC Core Principle 9 if deployed in the US.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: If Hyperliquid enters the US as Trump suggested, compliance (KYC, venue policing) would materially change its model.
insights.quote: These things can cascade and create market moving events. Because of the high leverage and the small amount of dollars.

insights.claim: Duffy claims the GPU market is already over $1 trillion and will be multiples of crypto's (under $3 trillion) size by 2030, and argues the administration is wrongly holding back CME's GPU futures on unexplained national-security grounds.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Compute derivatives are a large potential new asset class for CME pending regulatory approval; watch for approval as a catalyst.
insights.quote: The GPU you, market will be multiples of the size of crypto by 2030.

insights.claim: Duffy says 24/7 trading is inevitable because risk does not know what time it is, but the binding constraint is that the banking system must operate 24/7.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Round-the-clock trading in rates and equities is gated by banking/payment rails, not exchange tech.
insights.quote: 24/7 is inevitable and you can fight it.

insights.claim: Duffy notes the US equity market is about $76 trillion, which no one can pre-fund over a weekend while banks are closed, so rates and equities cannot trade 24/7 until banking does; small crypto markets can be pre-funded and CME already trades crypto 24/7.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Expect crypto first, equities/rates last in 24/7 rollout; Fed real-time payments are insufficient so far.
insights.quote: It's $76 trillion a market.

insights.claim: Duffy expects near-round-the-clock cash equities trading (transcribed as '2035', likely 23/5) to begin by the end of the year, a first for cash equities.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Extended-hours cash equity trading is imminent, with expected pockets of thin liquidity.

insights.claim: Duffy says the scariest moment of his career was April 20, 2020 when oil went to -$37.50, more frightening than 2008 because there was no assured government backstop and demand dried up instantly; CME had pre-listed negative-strike options to ensure price discovery.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Shows exchanges preparing for extreme price regimes; storage-driven dislocations can be more acute than credit crises.
insights.quote: I'll never forget April 20th of 2020, defending -3750 of oil and I was being crucified.

insights.claim: Duffy's core trading lesson, from going broke in 1981 after losing $50,000, is to know your exit before entering any trade and to accept being wrong.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy
insights.so_what: Risk-management discipline: define exit before entry.
insights.quote: before you get into something, you should know how to get out of it.
